results.title: TurboQuant Changes the Economics of Local AI Inference
results.content:
Numerous independent implementations. At least five different platforms. Consistent results. Implementations are already expanding beyond text LLMs: a vLLM plugin (`turboquant-vllm`) has been validated on vision-language models (Molmo2-4B/8B), where visual tokens create significantly higher KV cache pressure than text alone. The community-driven validation, without any code from Google, is itself a trust indicator. The results come from practitioners with no commercial incentive to inflate [...] and leaving no room for concurrent requests. After TurboQuant, the KV cache drops to about 1 GB. That frees 5 GB for a second concurrent user, or for extending the context to 200K tokens. One algorithm change. Same hardware. Twice the capacity. [...] Google Research published a blog post in March 2026 promoting TurboQuant , an algorithm available on arXiv since April 2025 and scheduled for presentation at ICLR 2026 in April . TurboQuant compresses the KV cache to as low as 3 bits, achieving at least 6x memory reduction in benchmark evaluations. No retraining. Near-zero accuracy degradation. For enterprise architects evaluating local inference, this changes the math.

results.title: TurboQuant on MLX: 4.6x KV Cache Compression with Custom Metal Kernels
results.content:
No layer-adaptive tricks needed on 32B. All 64 layers compressed, quality unchanged.

Memory savings at 16K context (32B): 4.2GB → 897MB. That’s 3.3GB freed up.

Qwen2.5–7B, speed across context lengths:

512 tokens: FP16=53, TQ3=49, ratio=0.91x

4K tokens: FP16=48, TQ3=46, ratio=0.97x

16K tokens: FP16=40, TQ3=38, ratio=0.96x

7B models are more sensitive — I keep first and last layers in FP16 (2.8x compression instead of 4.6x). 32B models don’t need this.

## WHAT ACTUALLY TOOK THE TIME [...] I also wrote a pre-rotated query kernel — instead of inverse-WHT on every cached K vector, apply forward-WHT once to Q and do codebook lookups directly. Saves the O(d log d) butterfly from the inner loop. Mathematically identical (verified cosine = 1.0 per head). [...] When I switched from uint8 indices to proper 3-bit packed uint32, the Python unpack loop made everything slower. Memory savings were real (4.6x) but decode went from 38 to 2.4 tok/s because unpacking happened in Python before the Metal dequant kernel.

Fix: moved the bit extraction into the Metal kernel. The GPU reads packed uint32 and extracts indices on the fly: (word >> (pos  3)) & 0x7. Zero Python overhead.

results.title: TurboQuant vs Traditional Model Quantization: What’s the Difference?
results.content:
TurboQuant applies quantization to KV cache tensors during inference.

Rather than compressing model weights, it compresses temporary runtime memory used by attention layers.

Reported research results show: [...] Approximately 3–4 bit KV-cache compression
   Common operating points near 3.5 bits per value
   Large reductions in KV-cache memory footprint
   Lower memory bandwidth pressure
   Higher throughput for long-context inference
   Near-zero measurable accuracy loss on benchmark evaluations

One of the notable findings is that compressed KV cache can retain quality close to full 16-bit precision.

results.content:
To understand TurboQuant’s significance, you first need to understand the KV cache bottleneck.

When a large language model generates text, it stores intermediate results — specifically, the Key and Value vectors from each attention head — in a dedicated memory buffer called the KV cache. This cache lets the model avoid recomputing everything for every new token, which would be computationally prohibitive .

## The Real Problem: KV Cache Growth

During inference, LLMs store intermediate representations called Key (K) and Value (V) vectors. This is known as the KV cache.

As more tokens are processed:

   KV cache keeps growing linearly
   Memory usage increases rapidly
   Attention computation becomes slower [...] Model size is fixed
   KV cache keeps growing

Now the real challenges are:

   Memory explosion
   Slower attention
   Higher inference cost

TurboQuant directly addresses all three.

## Where You’ll See TurboQuant Shine

TurboQuant is especially useful in scenarios like:

   Chat applications with long conversations
   RAG pipelines with large documents
   AI agents with memory
   Running LLMs on limited GPUs [...] This becomes a serious issue in:

   Long conversations
   RAG systems
   Agent workflows

And here’s the key point: Quantization does not solve this problem.

## TurboQuant: A Different Approach

_TurboQuant tackles the KV cache directly._

Instead of storing full precision vectors, it compresses them into a much smaller representation (around ~3 bits per value) and reconstructs them when needed.
